name: flurry (port of Java's ConcurrentHashMap)
baseline: RwLock<HashMap> (parking_lot RwLock around std HashMap in the measurements)
verdict_reason: flurry beats a single RwLock<HashMap> on a read-heavy mix at high thread counts (about 6.9x at 16 threads), but is slower on one thread, about 4x behind DashMap on the insert/remove-heavy mix, and was killed for running out of memory in one run. Its own README now steers users to papaya or dashmap.
tier_reason: Independent results (leapfrog's fork of conc-map-bench) with public code, CPU, OS and build flags stated.
claimed_speedup: Read-heavy, FxHash, Ryzen 9 3950X: 80.8 vs 11.7 Mops/s at 16 threads (about 6.9x, derived from page data), 11.2 vs 19.4 at 1 thread; Apple M2 Max: 64.5 vs 3.4 at 12 threads. Exchange mix with SipHash at 16 threads: 9627180.87311915 ops/s vs 40457181.8270502 for DashMap.
workload: bustle harness with u64 keys: read-heavy (98% reads) and exchange (10% read, 40% insert, 40% remove, 10% update).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (16 cores); Apple M2 Max (12 cores)
toolchain: nightly Rust (2022), lto = true, codegen-units = 1; flurry 0.3.1
one_liner: Rust port of Java's ConcurrentHashMap; scales on reads but has memory and write-throughput problems its author acknowledges.
how_it_is_fast: Reads are lock-free: bins are reached through atomic pointers and memory is reclaimed with epoch-based garbage collection, so readers never block. Writers lock only the bin they modify, and resizing is cooperative across threads.
use_it_when: Rarely: read-mostly maps where you specifically want Java ConcurrentHashMap semantics.
skip_it_when: Most new code: the author recommends papaya or dashmap.
Insert/remove-heavy workloads, where it trailed DashMap by about 4x and one run ran out of memory.
Single-threaded or lightly contended access, where RwLock<HashMap> was faster.
caveats: Measured flurry 0.3.1 in 2022; the current release is 0.5.2.
Baseline was parking_lot's RwLock, before std's RwLock moved to futexes on Linux in Rust 1.62.
tradeoffs: Epoch-based reclamation delays freeing memory and raised memory use under load.
Every value access goes through a guard.
